title: Composting: Nature's Most Interesting Process
summary: Josh and Chuck explain composting as a way to divert food and yard waste from landfills, where anaerobic decomposition produces methane, a potent greenhouse gas. They cover choosing a site, bin structures (single and three-bin systems, tumbler), what to add and avoid (greens vs. browns, meat and dairy, pesticide-treated plants, invasive weeds, wood ash), carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, aeration and moisture, the microbial and food-web process through mesophilic, thermophilic and curing phases, and how to tell when compost is finished. The episode closes with a listener mail about childlife specialists responding to an earlier pain scale episode. Also a short note on the show's 'selects' series is included in the opening.

segments.title: Selects series announcement and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh explains the show is now running hand-selected classic episodes on Saturdays. The hosts chat about a Simpsons Halloween joke and Seattle.

segments.title: Food waste, landfills and methane
segments.summary: Hosts note that food makes up a large share of US landfill trash. In anaerobic landfill conditions it produces methane, a much more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide. Composting mostly produces carbon dioxide and diverts waste, extending landfill life.

segments.title: Composting basics and recycling rates
segments.summary: Hosts discuss municipal recycling rates including composting, Seattle's mandatory composting, and that composting ranges from city programs to home backyard piles. Composting needs organic material, soil microbes, moisture, and oxygen. Hosts describe the process as breaking matter into nutrients for plants.

segments.title: Active versus passive piles
segments.summary: A passive pile left unmanaged will decompose anaerobically and produce methane. Turning the pile or spraying it with a hose adds oxygen. Hosts call the unmanaged approach a doobie pile and discuss humus versus hummus.

segments.title: Choosing a compost site and bin structures
segments.summary: Advice on site selection: away from the house but close enough to tend, downwind, under a deciduous tree, with good drainage, on dirt rather than concrete, and checking local rules. Structures include bought or built bins, the single-bin system where finished compost collects at the bottom, and the three-bin system that needs active management. Tumbler bins are also mentioned.

segments.title: What to compost and what to avoid
segments.summary: Good inputs include kitchen scraps like banana peels, apple cores, coffee grounds with filters, napkins, newspaper, corn cobs, leaves, and shrub trimmings, chopped small. Seaweed and kelp rinsed of salt are good, as is sawdust. Avoid night soil, cat litter, diseased plants, invasive weeds such as buttercup, morning glory, and quack grass, and pesticide-treated plants. Meat and dairy are debated, and wood ash is cautioned as highly alkaline.

segments.title: Carbon to nitrogen ratio, greens and browns, aeration
segments.summary: Hosts explain the roughly 30 to 1 carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, with green recently deceased material high in nitrogen and dry brown material high in carbon. Too much nitrogen produces ammonia and odor; carbon breaks down slowly. Grass clippings are high in nitrogen. Oxygen should stay around ten percent or higher, and turning, a crank barrel, or perforated PVC pipes can aerate. Moisture should be damp, not soaking.

segments.title: Microbes, worms and the compost food web
segments.summary: Bacteria break down food waste using oxygen to produce energy, releasing carbon dioxide and heat. Earthworms and nematodes eat organic matter and aerate the pile. Primary, secondary and tertiary consumers, including mites, slugs, millipedes and predators, form a food web.

segments.title: Temperature phases of composting and finished compost
segments.summary: A compost pile moves through mesophilic, thermophilic and curing phases, heating to fifty to sixty degrees Celsius in the thermophilic stage, which kills pathogens. Temperatures above about sixty-five Celsius kill microbes. Finished compost is dark, crumbly and earthy-smelling, and can be used as fertilizer on gardens and trees.

segments.title: Using finished compost and curbside pickup
segments.summary: Finished compost improves soil microbes, nutrients, pH and structure. Towns are beginning curbside food waste pickup. Listeners are directed to resources including Cornell's composting site.

segments.title: Listener mail on child life specialists
segments.summary: A listener, a childlife specialist, explains the job of supporting hospitalized children and families and how to become certified. Another listener from Auburn University also writes in. The hosts had earlier discussed pain scales.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and give social media and website contact information.
